en: It's two in the morning on a night train... the lights are off, the A-C is humming, and your whole family is asleep on the berths.
visual: REAL: sleeper coach at night, blue night lamp, curtains swaying, a child asleep on a lower berth (Indian stock).
sound: Cold open: coach rattle, A-C hum, no music

en: Up front, one loco pilot is staring into the dark — watching for a signal that might be red.
visual: REAL: night locomotive cab POV, rain on the windscreen, wiper sweeping; distant signal glow.

en: Then one morning there's news of a train crash, and by lunchtime your family WhatsApp group is on fire.
visual: SIM: phone lock screen on a kitchen table, WhatsApp family group previews stacking up (generic names, no real accounts).
sound: Phone buzz on wood, pings layering

en: One forward says the government never bothered with safety, and another says India already has Kavach, so crashes should be impossible now.
visual: SIM: two forwards side by side: NO KAVACH? WHY? and KAVACH = ZERO ACCIDENTS.

en: Both forwards are playing with your fear — and both are missing what really happens on the track.
visual: Both forwards crack like glass; push through the crack into a dark track bed at night.

en: Welcome to Be Practical with Kishore.
visual: Kishore on camera / channel face card over the track bed; logo sting.

en: Today we'll open the railway's own documents, do the braking maths together, and read the official accident inquiries.
visual: PROOF: R-D-S-O spec cover, CRS abstract cover, PIB release, each sliding in on paper texture under a highlighter sweep.

en: And around the eight minute mark, I'll show you what the official inquiry reports actually found — and the honest answer to the hardest question of all... could Kavach have saved Balasore, or the Kanchanjunga Express?
visual: REAL: credited news stills of Bahanaga Bazar and Rangapani wreck sites under a forensic magnifier; a small minute counter ticks toward 8:00.
pacing: OPEN LOOP: re-check the minute against align/ before render

en: Let's start with what Kavach actually is — because it isn't an app, and nobody can switch it on across India overnight.
visual: SIM: an app icon labelled KAVACH dissolves into steel hardware; a big switch flips and nothing on the India map lights up.

en: Kavach is India's own Automatic Train Protection system. It watches the train's speed and the signals ahead, and if the train goes too fast or is about to pass a red signal, it warns the loco pilot... then brakes by itself if nothing changes.
visual: ILLUSTRATION (Engine 1, hardware X-ray): a train on a 3D track; permitted speed and the next signal float above the cab; WARNING flashes. Then the brake command flows into the brake pipe and the speed dial falls.

en: In March twenty twenty two, in a test in Telangana with the Railway Minister on board, Kavach stopped two engines running towards each other on the same line, about three hundred and eighty metres apart.
visual: REAL: March 2022 Kavach head-on trial footage (Ministry of Railways / PIB), credited.

en: It looks like magic on video. But Kavach is a chain of four links, and it only protects you when every link is in place.
visual: ILLUSTRATION: four glowing links snap together around a train.
pacing: Links snap in one by one

en: Link one sits on the track — small R-F-I-D tags fixed to the concrete sleepers, which a reader under the engine reads as it passes, so the train knows exactly where it is and on which line.
visual: REAL: RFID tag on a PSC sleeper (railway media); Engine 1 X-ray shows the under-chassis reader passing over it, tag ID and track ID popping up.
pacing: Low tracking shot along the sleepers

en: People say there's one tag every kilometre. Actually, one kilometre is only the longest gap allowed — near signals, points and stations the tags crowd together, and on one stretch of about ninety six kilometres between Vadodara and Ahmedabad, the railway fixed two thousand eight hundred and seventy two of them.
visual: ILLUSTRATION: evenly spaced dots get a red cross, then cluster around a signal and a turnout; BOARD: 2,872 ÷ 96 ≈ 30 per km over a map of the stretch.

en: Link two is the station. A Kavach computer there reads the signals, the points and which tracks are occupied, straight from the station's own signalling system — called interlocking. Remember that word.
visual: REAL: station relay room / Kavach equipment (railway media); ILLUSTRATION: interlocking panel lines feed into the Kavach box; the word INTERLOCKING stays lit.

en: Link three is the radio. Tall towers along the line carry messages between the station and the engine over a U-H-F safety radio... it's not your mobile network, and it's not five G.
visual: REAL: Kavach lattice tower beside the track (railway media); radio pulses animate to the cab; a 5G badge greys out.

en: And link four rides inside the engine — a Kavach computer, R-F-I-D readers, wheel speed sensors, a screen for the loco pilot, and a link to the brakes.
visual: ILLUSTRATION (Engine 1): the loco shell peels away layer by layer; each part labels in.

en: Think about that for a second — this is a system designed in India, by Indian engineers and Indian companies, for Indian tracks.
visual: REAL: R-D-S-O Lucknow campus / Indian engineers at a test bench (credited railway media).

en: The electronics are built to S-I-L four, the highest safety level in railway signalling. Some posts say that means Kavach can fail only once in a billion hours... that's only half the story, because it's a strict limit for each safety function of the electronics, not a promise that no train will ever crash.
visual: PROOF: SIL-4 band on a standards page under the magnifier. Then SIM: viral post ONE FAILURE IN A BILLION HOURS stamped HALF THE STORY.

en: So keep this one in your pocket... Kavach can only act on the information it's given.
visual: ILLUSTRATION: data arrow from interlocking into Kavach glows, then holds.

en: Now, if Kavach can see the red signal, why can't the loco pilot just slam the brakes, the way you would in a car?
visual: REAL: locomotive approaching head-on, low angle; cut to a car braking on an Indian road.

en: Because steel wheels on a steel rail have very little grip, a train is enormously heavy, and when the brakes go on, the air pressure has to change all the way down the brake pipe to the last coach.
visual: REAL: wheel on rail macro with sparks; ILLUSTRATION: an air-pressure wave travels down the brake pipe coach by coach.
pacing: Wave runs the length of the rake

en: Here's a real number from the railway's own training notes. A Vande Bharat running at one hundred and thirty kilometres per hour needs about six hundred and fifty metres to stop... even with its emergency brakes.
visual: PROOF: IRIMEE Vande Bharat braking table under the magnifier; REAL: Vande Bharat at speed; ILLUSTRATION (Engine 2): speed falls along a 654 m track ruler.
onscreen: VANDE BHARAT · 130 KM/H · EMERGENCY BRAKE 654 M
pacing: Ruler draws ahead of the train

en: At that speed, it covers about thirty six metres every single second.
visual: BOARD: 130 ÷ 3.6 ≈ 36 m per second.

en: Now picture a loaded goods train — five thousand tonnes at seventy five kilometres per hour. Its brakes build up slowly, and simple maths with fair guesses gives more than nine hundred metres to stop.
visual: REAL: loaded freight train, long rake of wagons; BOARD: d = v·t + v²/2a worked live, ≈ 930 m, labelled ILLUSTRATIVE MODEL.

en: And if you push the speed from one hundred and thirty to one hundred and sixty, the braking distance doesn't grow by a little... it grows by about half.
visual: BOARD: (160/130)² ≈ 1.5; Engine 2 curve stretches.

en: Now add a December night in north India, with thick fog on the tracks.
visual: REAL: dense winter fog over a north Indian track at night.

en: Suppose the loco pilot can see a signal only fifty metres ahead. At one hundred and ten kilometres per hour, the train crosses those fifty metres in less than two seconds — and even an alert person needs a second or two just to react. On eyes alone, the maths simply doesn't work.
visual: ILLUSTRATION (Engine 3, fog split): a signal appears out of fog at 50 m; a stopwatch runs out at 1.6 s.

en: This is where Kavach changes the game. It doesn't wait for anyone to see the red signal — it already knows how far away it is, shows it on the screen inside the cab, and brakes early while there's still enough room.
visual: ILLUSTRATION (Engine 3 right half + Engine 2): cab display shows the aspect and target distance long before it is visible; the braking curve is drawn ahead of the train and the Kavach brake point lands well before the signal.

en: But it can't cancel physics. If danger appears closer than the stopping distance, even Kavach can't stop the train in time.
visual: ILLUSTRATION: an obstacle appears inside the curve; the zone turns crimson.

en: And how often does a train pass a red signal by mistake? The Commission of Railway Safety noted two hundred and eight such cases in five years, from April twenty nineteen to March twenty twenty four... and twelve of them ended in a collision.
visual: PROOF: CRS abstract page under the magnifier, highlighter on the line; counter rolls to 208, then 12 turns red.

en: So why isn't it on every track yet? Look at the size of the job. Indian Railways runs about sixty nine thousand route kilometres, and in March twenty twenty five it had about sixteen thousand diesel and electric engines.
visual: ILLUSTRATION (Engine 4): national rail map draws in grey across India; REAL: loco shed with rows of engines.
pacing: Map draws in, cut to shed

en: By the end of July twenty twenty six, the newest Kavach was working on two thousand six hundred and thirty three route kilometres, on parts of the Delhi Mumbai and Delhi Howrah routes — two of the busiest in the country.
visual: ILLUSTRATION (Engine 4): two corridors glow cyan; labels 1,423 km and 1,210 km.

en: Add the older version on about one thousand four hundred and sixty five kilometres in South Central Railway, and Kavach is still working on well under a tenth of the network.
visual: Map: SCR section glows in a second colour; BOARD: (2,633 + 1,465) ÷ 69,439 < 10%.

en: And here's the trap in most headlines. Track fitted with equipment, seven thousand seven hundred and twenty six kilometres, engines fitted, six thousand two hundred and ninety, and track where work has only started, twenty one thousand seven hundred and ninety four kilometres... but fitted isn't working, and work started isn't protected.
visual: SIM: headlines blurred except the numbers; funnel tiers fill FITTED 7,726 · LOCOS 6,290 · WORK STARTED 21,794, then narrow to the thin working stream; stamp FITTED ≠ WORKING.
onscreen: FITTED 7,726 · LOCOS 6,290 · WORK STARTED 21,794 · FITTED ≠ WORKING

en: The money is moving too — the yearly Kavach budget rose from about one thousand one hundred crore rupees to about one thousand six hundred and seventy crore in twenty twenty five twenty six.
visual: ILLUSTRATION: two budget bars rise.

en: But money alone doesn't make it work. Every station's signalling data has to be checked, every engine type wired to its own brakes, the radio has to reach every yard, and then it's all tested and retested before a single kilometre is called working.
visual: REAL: signalling technicians at a relay rack; ILLUSTRATION (flowchart): survey → data → loco fitment → radio → integrated trials looping back on failure → COMMISSIONED.

en: Suppliers are the other bottleneck. For years, just three Indian companies made Kavach — Medha, H-B-L and Kernex — and a newer one, Quadrant Future Tek, told the stock exchange it got permission for passenger trials only in May twenty twenty six.
visual: PROOF: official list naming the three firms, then the company's exchange filing under the magnifier; stamp NOT FINAL APPROVAL.
onscreen: MEDHA · HBL · KERNEX · PASSENGER TRIALS ≠ FINAL APPROVAL
pacing: Magnifier pan, highlighter on the line
cite: [PIB | MAR 2025 · IEI | SEP 2024 · NSE FILING | 26 MAY 2026]

en: Now, the question I promised you at the start.
visual: Black frame, slow fade up on twisted coaches (credited archive).

en: Case one. Bahanaga Bazar, near Balasore in Odisha, June two, twenty twenty three. The Coromandel Express is coming in at about one hundred and twenty eight kilometres per hour, on a green signal for the main line.
visual: REAL: credited archive of the Bahanaga Bazar site; map pin; ILLUSTRATION (Engine 5, logic gate): station layout, train arrow on the up main line, home signal turns green.

en: But the crossover ahead is set towards the loop line... where a goods train is standing.
visual: Engine 5: crossover 17A/B swings to the loop; the parked goods train is highlighted. ILLUSTRATION.

en: The official inquiry found lapses in signalling circuit work done at the station. Close to three hundred people lost their lives.
visual: PROOF: CRS abstract finding under the magnifier, highlighter on the line; then a slow push on a memorial / candles still (credited), no victims shown.

en: So, would Kavach have stopped it?
visual: Engine 5: a Kavach box appears on the loco and pulses.
sound: Total music silence 1.5 s after this line, then a low braam

en: Here's the honest answer — nobody can say yes or no for sure.
visual: Kishore / dark track bed.

en: Remember interlocking? At Balasore, the signalling system itself was showing a false green, and fed that same wrong information, Kavach could have believed the line was clear too.
visual: Engine 5: the false green travels down the wire into Kavach, which shows green too. ILLUSTRATION.

en: A safety computer can't correct wrong information it trusts. Kavach does have a few checks of its own, but no public study has shown whether they would have acted in time there.
visual: Engine 5: both channels agree on the wrong input; tag reads appear on the loop line, dotted and uncertain.

en: So the forward saying Kavach would surely have saved Balasore, and the one saying it surely couldn't, are both going beyond the evidence.
visual: The two forwards from the hook return, both stamped BEYOND THE EVIDENCE.

en: Case two. Rangapani, near New Jalpaiguri in north Bengal, June seventeen, twenty twenty four. The automatic signals had failed, so trains were moving on a paper authority, at a slow, careful speed.
visual: REAL: credited archive of the Rangapani site; map pin; ILLUSTRATION (Engine 6): a row of automatic signals goes dark; a generic paper authority slides in (no copy of a real form).

en: The inquiry found the goods train was handed the wrong form, T-A nine one two instead of T-D nine one two, with no caution order, missing walkie talkies, and training that wasn't good enough... failures of the system, not just one loco pilot.
visual: ILLUSTRATION: two distinct labels T/A 912 and T/D 912, the wrong one highlighted; three items tick red around the station building: caution order, walkie-talkie, training.

en: The goods train reached seventy eight kilometres per hour and hit the Kanchanjunga Express from behind at about forty. And there was no working Kavach on that section.
visual: Engine 6: freight speed trace climbs to 78, collision marked at about 40; map overlay shows no Kavach line here.

en: Here, Kavach could have made a real difference. With both trains fitted and the section working, it could have held the goods train to the allowed movement and a slow speed past those failed signals.
visual: Engine 6 rewinds; a Kavach box appears on both locos; freight speed is held low and the braking curve stops it short. SIMULATION.

en: And that famous claim that Kavach always locks the speed at exactly fifteen? Fifteen is the rule loco pilots follow at failed signals — what Kavach enforces depends on its data and settings, so don't take that number as a promise.
visual: SIM: viral claim card stamped DEPENDS ON SET-UP.

en: Two crashes, two different failures. At Balasore the signalling information itself was wrong, at Kanchanjunga the backup rules broke down — and Kavach is strongest against the second kind.
visual: Side-by-side comparison: two columns, two icons; then REAL: a technician testing a relay rack.

en: So what can you actually do with all this? Three things.
visual: REAL: dawn, a train crossing a bridge; three step markers appear in a lower corner.

en: One. When a Kavach forward lands in your family group, ask three questions before sharing it — is the number about fitted equipment or Kavach that's working, which date is it from, and was the problem a human mistake or wrong signalling data?
visual: SIM: the WhatsApp forward from the hook; three question chips pop beside it one by one.
onscreen: 1 · FITTED OR WORKING? · WHICH DATE? · HUMAN OR SIGNAL DATA?

en: Two. Read the real thing instead. The railway ministry posts Kavach progress in press releases on the P-I-B website, and the Commission of Railway Safety puts its inquiry findings on its own website, free to read.
visual: PROOF: screen recording of the PIB release page and the CRS website abstracts page (credited), highlighter on the Kavach paragraph.

en: Three. If you see something unsafe on a train or at a station, report it to Rail Madad by calling one three nine, or through the Rail Madad app.
visual: REAL: phone dialling 139 on a platform; Rail Madad app screen (credited).

en: Kavach isn't magic, and it isn't useless. It's an Indian-built safety layer that brakes early when a human slips... as long as the engine is fitted, the track section is working, the signalling data is right, and there's enough room to stop.
visual: The two myths from the hook fade out; the four links from Act 2 relight one by one: ENGINE · TRACK · DATA · DISTANCE.

en: Real safety isn't built on slogans. It's built by engineers and track crews doing careful, boring work right, every single day — and citizens who understand that keep the system accountable.
visual: REAL: track maintenance gang at work at sunrise; relay room; a Kavach loco rolling out at dawn.

en: Tell me in the comments: which route do you travel most, and do you know if Kavach is working on it yet?
